account: In September 2023 a report of the Virginia Transportation Research Council on wildlife crossings for Corridor Q estimated the societal cost of an elk crash, including monetized pain and suffering, at $80,771.49 in 2020 dollars. The Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT) later sponsored a one-year pilot by the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute (VTTI) on Route 460 near Grundy in Southwest Virginia, as part of the Corridor Q expansion. VDOT names the pilot the Animal Detection and Driver Warning System, and its project page identifies VTTI as the research partner. The page gave an estimated start of February 2025 and an estimated completion of September 2026 for the study. Eight portable solar-powered trailers with thermal cameras were installed on a 750-meter section of a 14-mile corridor that is home to about 100 elk. AI software from Crosstek analyzed the camera feeds. When the software detected wildlife, dynamic message signs told motorists that wildlife had been detected ahead and to slow down. T-Mobile provided 5G and satellite links. WCYB reported the test on 19 November 2025. In its separate interview, Michelle Earl of VDOT described animal detection and communication with the message boards. The pilot ended in September 2026. Gwen Sheldon reported the results for Virginia Tech on 20 October 2026. The system achieved 97 percent overall accuracy in identifying medium and large wildlife. In the initial analysis the researchers found an average speed reduction of 3 mph as vehicles approached activated signs. Virginia Tech reports that the team collected data on more than 10,000 passing vehicles and that data analysis was continuing after the pilot ended. Virginia Tech reports no result on collisions or fatalities prevented. Its report identifies Crosstek as the supplier of the cameras and the AI software. The measured results come from Virginia Tech's own report, and WCYB's earlier interview describes only the deployment.

fields.account: In September 2023 a report of the Virginia Transportation Research Council on wildlife crossings for Corridor Q estimated the societal cost of an elk crash, including monetized pain and suffering, at $80,771.49 in 2020 dollars. The Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT) later sponsored a one-year pilot by the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute (VTTI) on Route 460 near Grundy in Southwest Virginia, as part of the Corridor Q expansion. VDOT names the pilot the Animal Detection and Driver Warning System, and its project page identifies VTTI as the research partner. The page gave an estimated start of February 2025 and an estimated completion of September 2026 for the study. Eight portable solar-powered trailers with thermal cameras were installed on a 750-meter section of a 14-mile corridor that is home to about 100 elk. AI software from Crosstek analyzed the camera feeds. When the software detected wildlife, dynamic message signs told motorists that wildlife had been detected ahead and to slow down. T-Mobile provided 5G and satellite links. WCYB reported the test on 19 November 2025. In its separate interview, Michelle Earl of VDOT described animal detection and communication with the message boards. The pilot ended in September 2026. Gwen Sheldon reported the results for Virginia Tech on 20 October 2026. The system achieved 97 percent overall accuracy in identifying medium and large wildlife. In the initial analysis the researchers found an average speed reduction of 3 mph as vehicles approached activated signs. Virginia Tech reports that the team collected data on more than 10,000 passing vehicles and that data analysis was continuing after the pilot ended. Virginia Tech reports no result on collisions or fatalities prevented. Its report identifies Crosstek as the supplier of the cameras and the AI software. The measured results come from Virginia Tech's own report, and WCYB's earlier interview describes only the deployment.
